title: Why it helps to eat lunch away from your desk
dek: Research on lunch breaks links mentally stepping away from work to less exhaustion over time. Here is how to make a short break count.
keyPoints: A 12-month study of 841 workers found that mentally detaching from work at lunch was linked to lower exhaustion and more vigor a year later.
Having control over how you spend the break also helped recovery.
For screen-tired eyes, the American Optometric Association suggests looking 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes.
The same group recommends a 15-minute eye rest after two hours of continuous screen work.

sources.title: Recovery during Lunch Breaks: Testing Long-Term Relations with Energy Levels at Work | Scandinavian Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology

body: Eating over the keyboard feels efficient, and for many people it is the default. The trouble is that you never really leave work, so the afternoon starts with the same tired brain you had at noon.

Researchers who followed 841 employees in Finland for a year looked at what made a lunch break restful. The strongest factor was psychological detachment, meaning the worker stopped thinking about work during the break. People whose lunches helped them recover reported less exhaustion and more vigor twelve months later. Having some control over how they spent the break mattered too.

That suggests the location matters mostly because it helps you switch off. A break room, a kitchen table or a bench outside all work if the email stays closed. Scrolling work messages on your phone at a picnic table is still working.

Your eyes get a break as well. The American Optometric Association recommends the 20-20-20 rule for screen work, which means looking at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, plus a 15-minute rest after two hours of continuous computer use. A lunch away from the monitor covers the longer rest without any extra effort.

Some days a real break is not possible, and that is fine. When it is, pick a spot away from your desk today, set your phone to silent, and give yourself at least fifteen minutes with no work on the screen.
